title: Section 2305.10 | Bodily injury or injury to personal property.
content:
## Ohio Revised Code § 2305.10 — Bodily injury or injury to personal property

### Division (A): General limitations period

- Except as provided in divisions **(C)** or **(E)**:
  - An action based on a **product liability claim**; and
  - An action for **bodily injury** or **injuring personal property**
  - “shall be brought within two years after the cause of action accrues.”
- Except as provided in divisions **(B)(1), (2), (3), (4), and (5)**:
  - A cause of action accrues “when the injury or loss to person or property occurs.”

### Division (B): Accrual for specified exposures

For each category below, the cause of action accrues on the earlier of:

- The date on which the plaintiff is informed by competent medical authority that the plaintiff has an injury related to the exposure; or
- The date on which, by exercising reasonable diligence, the plaintiff should have known that the plaintiff has an injury related to the exposure.

| Division | Exposure or injury |
|---|---|
| **(B)(1)** | Bodily injury caused by exposure to hazardous or toxic chemicals, ethical drugs, or ethical medical devices, except bodily injuries described in divisions (B)(2), (3), (4), or (5). |
| **(B)(2)** | Bodily injury caused by exposure to chromium in any of its chemical forms. |
| **(B)(3)** | Bodily injury incurred by a veteran through exposure to chemical defoliants or herbicides or other causative agents, including agent orange. |
| **(B)(4)** | Bodily injury caused by exposure to diethylstilbestrol or other nonsteroidal synthetic estrogens, including exposure before birth. |
| **(B)(5)** | Bodily injury caused by exposure to asbestos. |

### Division (C): Product-liability ten-year limitation

#### Division (C)(1)

Except as otherwise provided in divisions **(C)(2), (3), (4), (5), (6), and (7)** or in **section 2305.19 of the Revised Code**:

- “No cause of action based on a product liability claim shall accrue against the manufacturer or supplier of a product later than ten years” from the date the product was delivered to:
  - Its first purchaser; or
  - Its first lessee;
- The purchaser or lessee must not have been engaged in a business in which the product was used as a component in the:
  - Production;
  - Construction;
  - Creation;
  - Assembly; or
  - Rebuilding of another product.

#### Division (C)(2): Fraud exception

Division (C)(1) does not apply if:

- The manufacturer or supplier engaged in fraud regarding information about the product; and
- The fraud contributed to the alleged harm in a product liability claim involving that product.

#### Division (C)(3): Express written warranty exception

Division (C)(1) does not bar an action against a manufacturer or supplier that:

- Made an express, written warranty as to the safety of the product;
- Made the warranty for a period longer than ten years; and
- At the time the cause of action accrued, the warranty had not expired according to its terms.

#### Division (C)(4): Cause accruing less than two years before ten-year expiration

If:

- The cause of action concerning a product liability claim accrues during the ten-year period described in division (C)(1); and
- The cause of action accrues less than two years before that period expires;

Then:

- The product liability action may be commenced within two years after the cause of action accrues.

#### Division (C)(5): Disability exception

If:

- A cause of action concerning a product liability claim accrues during the ten-year period described in division (C)(1); and
- The claimant cannot commence an action during that period because of a disability described in **section 2305.16 of the Revised Code**;

Then:

- The product liability action may be commenced within two years after the disability is removed.

#### Division (C)(6): Asbestos exception

Division (C)(1) does not bar an action for bodily injury caused by exposure to asbestos if the cause of action accrues on the earlier of:

- The date on which the plaintiff is informed by competent medical authority that the plaintiff has an injury related to the exposure; or
- The date on which, by exercising reasonable diligence, the plaintiff should have known that the plaintiff has an injury related to the exposure.

#### Division (C)(7): Certain bodily-injury product-liability claims

##### Division (C)(7)(a)

Division (C)(1) does not bar an action against a manufacturer or supplier of a product if all of the following apply:

1. “The action is for bodily injury.”
2. The product is a substance or device described in division **(B)(1), (2), (3), or (4)**.
3. The bodily injury results from exposure to the product during the ten-year period described in division (C)(1).

##### Division (C)(7)(b)

When division (C)(7)(a) applies:

- The cause of action accrues on the earlier of:
  - The date on which the claimant is informed by competent medical authority that the bodily injury was related to exposure to the product; or
  - The date on which, by exercising reasonable diligence, the claimant should have known that the bodily injury was related to exposure to the product.
- The product liability action:
  - “Shall be commenced within two years after the cause of action accrues”; and
  - “Shall not be commenced more than two years after the cause of action accrues.”

### Division (D): No new cause of action

- “This section does not create a new cause of action or substantive legal right against any person involving a product liability claim.”

### Division (E): Childhood sexual abuse

- An action brought by a victim of childhood sexual abuse asserting any claim resulting from childhood sexual abuse, as defined in **section 2305.111 of the Revised Code**, “shall be brought as provided in division (C) of that section.”

### Division (F): Definitions

| Term | Definition stated in the section |
|---|---|
| **“Agent orange,” “causative agent,” and “veteran”** | Have the same meanings as in **section 5903.21 of the Revised Code**. |
| **“Ethical drug,” “ethical medical device,” “manufacturer,” “product,” “product liability claim,” and “supplier”** | Have the same meanings as in **section 2307.71 of the Revised Code**. |
| **“Harm”** | Means “injury, death, or loss to person or property.” |

### Division (G): Remedial application

- The section “shall be considered to be purely remedial in operation.”
- It “shall be applied in a remedial manner” in any civil action:
  - Commenced on or after **April 7, 2005**;
  - In which the section is relevant;
  - Regardless of when the cause of action accrued; and
  - Notwithstanding any other section of the Revised Code or prior rule of law of Ohio.
- It “shall not be construed to apply to any civil action pending prior to April 7, 2005.”

title: Section 2315.33 | Contributory fault effect on right to recover.
content:
## Ohio Revised Code § 2315.33 — Contributory Fault Effect on Right to Recover

| Item | Official information |
|---|---|
| Section | Section 2315.33 |
| Title | “Contributory fault effect on right to recover.” |
| Effective date | April 7, 2005 |
| Latest legislation | Senate Bill 80 – 125th General Assembly |
| Recovery rule | “The contributory fault of a person does not bar the person as plaintiff from recovering damages that have directly and proximately resulted from the tortious conduct of one or more other persons” if the statutory threshold is met. |
| Recovery threshold | The plaintiff’s contributory fault “was not greater than the combined tortious conduct of all other persons” from whom the plaintiff seeks recovery in the action and all other persons from whom the plaintiff does not seek recovery in the action. |
| Reduction of damages | “The court shall diminish any compensatory damages recoverable by the plaintiff by an amount that is proportionately equal to the percentage of tortious conduct of the plaintiff.” |
| Determination of plaintiff’s percentage of tortious conduct | Determined pursuant to section 2315.34 of the Revised Code. |

## Available Version

- April 7, 2005 – Senate Bill 80 – 125th General Assembly

title: Section 2315.18 | Compensatory damages in tort actions - factors excluded - findings or interrogatories.
content:
## Ohio Revised Code § 2315.18 — Compensatory damages in tort actions

### Definitions

- **“Asbestos claim”** has the same meaning as in § 2307.91 of the Revised Code.
- **“Economic loss”** means any of the following types of pecuniary harm:
  - “All wages, salaries, or other compensation lost as a result of an injury or loss to person or property that is a subject of a tort action.”
  - “All expenditures for medical care or treatment, rehabilitation services, or other care, treatment, services, products, or accommodations as a result of an injury or loss to person or property that is a subject of a tort action.”
  - “Any other expenditures incurred as a result of an injury or loss to person or property that is a subject of a tort action, other than attorney's fees incurred in connection with that action.”
- **“Medical claim,” “dental claim,” “optometric claim,” and “chiropractic claim”** have the same meanings as in § 2305.113 of the Revised Code.
- **“Noneconomic loss”** means “nonpecuniary harm that results from an injury or loss to person or property that is a subject of a tort action,” including, but not limited to:
  - Pain and suffering
  - Loss of society
  - Consortium
  - Companionship
  - Care
  - Assistance
  - Attention
  - Protection
  - Advice
  - Guidance
  - Counsel
  - Instruction
  - Training
  - Education
  - Disfigurement
  - Mental anguish
  - “Any other intangible loss”
- **“Occurrence”** means “all claims resulting from or arising out of any one person's bodily injury.”
- **“Product liability claim”** has the same meaning as in § 2307.71 of the Revised Code.
- **“Tort action”** means “a civil action for damages for injury or loss to person or property.”
  - It includes:
    - A civil action upon a product liability claim
    - A civil action upon an asbestos claim
    - A civil action based on an unlawful discriminatory practice relating to employment brought under § 4112.052 of the Revised Code
    - A civil action brought under § 4112.14 of the Revised Code
  - It does not include:
    - A civil action upon a medical claim
    - A civil action upon a dental claim
    - A civil action upon an optometric claim
    - A civil action upon a chiropractic claim
    - A civil action for damages for a breach of contract or another agreement between persons
- **“Trier of fact”** means “the jury or, in a nonjury action, the court.”

### Limits and operative rules

| Provision | Rule |
|---|---|
| Economic damages | “There shall not be any limitation on the amount of compensatory damages that represents the economic loss of the person who is awarded the damages in the tort action.” |
| Noneconomic damages | Except as provided in § 2315.18(B)(3), compensatory damages for recoverable noneconomic loss “shall not exceed the greater of two hundred fifty thousand dollars or an amount that is equal to three times the economic loss,” as determined by the trier of fact. |
| Per-plaintiff maximum | The three-times-economic-loss calculation is subject to “a maximum of three hundred fifty thousand dollars for each plaintiff in that tort action.” |
| Per-occurrence maximum | The three-times-economic-loss calculation is also subject to “a maximum of five hundred thousand dollars for each occurrence that is the basis of that tort action.” |

### No limitation on noneconomic damages

There is no limitation on compensatory damages representing recoverable noneconomic loss if the plaintiff’s noneconomic losses are for either of the following:

1. “Permanent and substantial physical deformity, loss of use of a limb, or loss of a bodily organ system.”
2. “Permanent physical functional injury that permanently prevents the injured person from being able to independently care for self and perform life-sustaining activities.”

### Evidence excluded when determining noneconomic damages

In determining an award of compensatory damages for noneconomic loss, the trier of fact “shall not consider”:

1. “Evidence of a defendant's alleged wrongdoing, misconduct, or guilt.”
2. “Evidence of the defendant's wealth or financial resources.”
3. “All other evidence that is offered for the purpose of punishing the defendant, rather than offered for a compensatory purpose.”

### Required findings or interrogatories

If a plaintiff prevails at trial in a tort action for injury or loss to person or property:

- In a **nonjury trial**, the court shall make findings of fact.
- In a **jury trial**, the jury shall return a general verdict accompanied by answers to interrogatories.

The findings or interrogatories shall specify:

1. “The total compensatory damages recoverable by the plaintiff.”
2. “The portion of the total compensatory damages that represents damages for economic loss.”
3. “The portion of the total compensatory damages that represents damages for noneconomic loss.”

### Entry of judgment

After the trier of fact complies with the required findings or interrogatories:

- The court shall enter judgment for compensatory damages for economic loss in the amount determined under § 2315.18(D)(2).
- Subject to § 2315.18(F)(1), the court shall enter judgment for compensatory damages for noneconomic loss.
- Except as provided in § 2315.18(B)(3), “in no event shall a judgment for compensatory damages for noneconomic loss exceed the maximum recoverable amount” under § 2315.18(B)(2).
- In a jury trial, § 2315.18(B) applies “only after the jury has made its factual findings and determination as to the damages.”

Before trial, any party may seek summary judgment concerning “the nature of the alleged injury or loss to person or property,” seeking a determination of damages under § 2315.18(B)(2).

### Court jurisdiction and jury instructions

- “A court of common pleas has no jurisdiction to enter judgment on an award of compensatory damages for noneconomic loss in excess of the limits set forth in this section.”
- If the trier of fact is a jury:
  - The court shall not instruct the jury regarding the § 2315.18(B)(2) limit on noneconomic damages.
  - Counsel for any party and witnesses shall not inform the jury or potential jurors of that limit.

### Reallocation of excess noneconomic damages

For a tort action to which § 2315.18(B)(2) applies:

- Any excess compensatory damages for noneconomic loss above the applicable amount specified in § 2315.18(B)(2) “shall not be reallocated to any other tortfeasor beyond the amount of compensatory damages that the tortfeasor would otherwise be responsible for under the laws of this state.”

### Actions excluded from § 2315.18

The section does not apply to:

1. Tort actions brought against the state in the court of claims, including actions in which a state university or college is a defendant and to which § 3345.40(B)(3) of the Revised Code applies.
2. Tort actions brought against political subdivisions of Ohio that are commenced under or subject to Chapter 2744. of the Revised Code. Section 2744.05(C) applies to recoverable damages in those actions.
3. Wrongful death actions brought under Chapter 2125. of the Revised Code.

### Constitutional provision

“If the provisions regarding the limits on compensatory damages for noneconomic loss set forth in division (B)(2) of this section have been determined to be unconstitutional,” § 2315.18(C) and § 2315.19 of the Revised Code govern the determination of an award of compensatory damages for noneconomic loss in a tort action.

title: Common Pleas, General Division
content:
## Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas, General Division

- **Mission Statement:** “As an equal and independent branch of government the Judges of the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas, acting with integrity, shall provide a safe, accessible, transparent, efficient, and impartial system of justice by fairly resolving disputes, respecting the public interest, and preserving individual rights while maintaining the rule of law.”
- **Diversity, Equity, & Inclusion Statement:** “Our commitment to diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility drives us forward to better.”
- **Pledge of Fairness:** “The fundamental mission of the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas is to provide a fair and impartial forum for the resolution of disputes according to the rule of law.”
- The Judges and staff “make this pledge to each litigant, defendant, victim, witness, juror, and person involved in a court proceeding”:
  - “Fairness includes the opportunity to be heard.”
  - “The chance to have the court process explained.”
  - “The right to be treated with respect.”

## Court and administrative sections listed

- Judges
- Administration
- Mediation and Alternative Dispute Resolution
- Common Pleas Magistrates
- Jury Commission
- Assignment Commission
- Local Rules
  - The page states: “Rule 31 has been changed as of 7/29/36.”
- Probation
- Specialized Dockets
- Virtual Help Center
- Pretrial Services
- Technology Plan

## Scam warning

“Scammers are actively impersonating personnel of the Hamilton County Sheriff's Office, Electronic Monitoring Unit and/or the Clerk of Courts, to call families of incarcerated individuals, claiming a fee is needed for immediate release via an electronic GPS ankle monitor.”

- The fraudulent calls:
  - “use spoofed numbers”
  - “often publicly available arrest records”
  - demand “quick, non-traceable payments through Zelle, Venmo or Cash App”
- “Hamilton County will never require payment of a fee for electronic monitoring services prior to release from the Justice Center.”
- Suspicious calls may be verified by contacting the **Electronic Monitoring Unit (EMU)** at **513-946-9800**.

## Official Safety Facts and Guidance Stated on the Page

### Sharing the Road

- “Stay alert and slow down in areas with heavy pedestrian or bicycle activity, especially at crosswalks and intersections.”
- “Give at least three feet of space when passing bicycles and motorcycles – allow a safe buffer and only pass when it’s legal and clear.”
- “Check blind spots carefully, as pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorcycles can be harder to see than cars.”

### Staying Focused and in the Lane

- “26% of Ohio’s fatal crashes over the last 5 years were the result of driving off the roadway.”
- “Driving off the road is the 2nd most common factor in teen crashes in Ohio. Speeding is #1.”
- “Distraction often causes drivers to drift out of their lane which puts themselves, their passengers, and others on the road in danger.”
- “Ohio’s distracted driving law makes it illegal to use or hold a cell phone in your hand or on your lap while driving.”

### RoadReady Ohio

- “RoadReady Ohio is a free app for new drivers that helps them log their required 50 hours of driving practice.”
- “Beginning April 1, 2026, the BMV will require new drivers to submit a detailed log of supervised driving hours with their 50 Hour Affidavit.”

## Reported Crash Narratives

### Driver Hospitalized After Hitting Parked Car on Howell Avenue

- On January 12, 2026, the driver of a white car was traveling south on Whitfield Avenue in Cincinnati and attempted to turn left onto Howell Avenue.
- He lost control and crossed the center line on Howell Avenue, hitting a parked car that was facing west on Howell Avenue.
- The white car continued onto the sidewalk where it hit a tree and a light pole.
- The driver was not wearing a seat belt and was taken to the hospital with serious injuries.
- His front seat passenger was wearing a seat belt and was not hurt.
- He was cited for:
  - Failure to Maintain Control
  - Failure to Wear a Seat Belt
- He also did not have a valid driver’s license.

### Speed a Factor in Chain Reaction Crash on I-275

- The driver of a black car was eastbound in the left lane of I-275 in wet conditions on February 19, 2026.
- She was traveling at 70 mph when she rear-ended a tan SUV that was stopped in traffic near mile post 33.
- The impact pushed the SUV into the back of a blue car ahead.
- The driver of the blue car continued eastbound and left the scene before authorities arrived.
- Both drivers were wearing seat belts and no injuries were reported.
- The driver of the black car was cited for Failure to Maintain Assured Clear Distance Ahead.
